statement: Neolithic sign-use candidates predating oracle bone script by millennia — Jiahu tortoise-shell/pottery symbols (c. 6600-6200 BCE, 11 identified symbols), Banpo pottery marks, and the Dinggong/Longshan potsherd (discovered 1992, 11-12 signs) — are NOT confirmed antecedents of Chinese writing by mainstream paleography. A 2003 Antiquity report on Jiahu (Li, Harbottle, Zhang, Wang) explicitly interprets the symbols "not as writing itself, but as features of a lengthy period of sign-use." Dinggong's Neolithic dating is itself disputed (Feng Shi 1994 argues for it; other scholars dispute the dating). These candidates remain archaeologically and functionally disconnected from Shang script.
scholarly_disagreement: Dinggong's dating and even its authenticity as a genuine Longshan-period inscription is actively disputed among specialists, not merely uncertain by default.

sources.citation: Li, X., G. Harbottle, J. Zhang, and C. Wang. "The earliest writing? Sign use in the seventh millennium BC at Jiahu, Henan Province, China." Antiquity 77 (2003).
Boltz, William G. The Origin and Early Development of the Chinese Writing System. American Oriental Series 78, Eisenbrauns, 1994.
sources.author: William G. Boltz

does_not_demonstrate: That oracle bone script has no undocumented antecedent development at all — Boltz notes the earliest oracle-bone script is already highly abstract and standardized, implying a real developmental gap not filled by these Neolithic finds
